summary: Salton City sits on the western shore of the Salton Sea — California's largest lake by surface area and one of its strangest environmental stories — yet most Californians couldn't place it on a map. The town sprawls across 21 square miles of flat, arid desert floor in the Imperial Valley, where summer highs routinely exceed 100°F and the annual average daily high lands at 86°F with nearly 11 hours of sunshine, making shade and air conditioning non-negotiable infrastructure. At a median home value of $189,800, prices look almost impossibly low by California standards, but a median household income of $36,915 means the price-to-income ratio still exceeds 5:1 — affordability is relative when wages are thin. This is not a job center; employment options nearby lean toward agriculture and public-sector roles concentrated further south in the Imperial Valley, so most working residents face long commutes. Grocery and dining options are sparse — no walkable commercial core, no evening sidewalk culture, just wide desert roads connecting scattered subdivisions to a few service-oriented businesses along the main highway. The landscape delivers genuinely dramatic desert sunsets over the Santa Rosa Mountains, and the Anza-Borrego Desert State Park boundary lies not far to the west. Salton City is less a conventional town than a desert grid of roads and lots where California's housing math briefly works on paper, though the infrastructure to support daily life remains thin.
